claims.text: A carefully controlled tempering heat treatment can induce a reversible ductile–brittle–ductile transition in conventional Cr–Mo low-alloy steel.
The reversible transition is produced by modulating impurity segregation at grain boundaries.
Cr–Mo low-alloy steel is ductile in its tempered state before the onset of temper embrittlement.
The proposed tempering schedule spans temperatures below, within, and above a narrow embrittlement window.
Temperatures within the embrittlement range activate impurity segregation in Cr–Mo low-alloy steel.
Annealing at higher temperatures reverses the effects of impurity segregation.
Grain-boundary impurity segregation at a specific temperature causes a dramatic loss of ductility.
At a critical tempering temperature, impurities segregate to grain boundaries and cause brittle behavior.
Further tempering at higher temperatures reverses grain-boundary impurity segregation.
Reversal of grain-boundary impurity segregation restores ductility.
Cr–Mo steel will change from ductile to brittle when tempered within the critical temperature window.
Cr–Mo steel will return to a ductile state upon further tempering outside the critical temperature window.
The embrittlement effect is confined to a narrow temperature window in which impurity segregation is sufficiently activated.
Below the segregation window, the material remains ductile because segregation has not occurred.
Above the segregation window, the material remains ductile because segregation has been reversed.
The temperature limits and kinetics of impurity segregation and reversal may vary with composition and processing conditions.

contradictions.description: The initial state is described as being before the onset of embrittlement, while the baseline calls the same initially ductile steel 'temper-embrittled.'
